plain_english: When we're talking about the happy life, you can't just tell me "Most people agree with this view" as if we were voting in Congress. That's exactly why it's probably wrong. Things aren't going so well with humanity that the majority picks the better path. In fact, the more people do something, the worse it usually is. So let's ask a different question. Not "What do most people do?" but "What should we do? What will give us lasting happiness?" Don't ask what the masses approve of — they're terrible guides to truth. And by "the masses" I mean both the poor in wool cloaks and the rich wearing crowns. I don't judge people by their clothes. I don't trust my eyes to tell me who someone really is. I have a better, more reliable light to tell truth from lies: let the mind discover what's good for the mind.
original_excerpt: When we are considering a happy life, you cannot answer me as though after a division of the House, "This view has most supporters;" because for that very reason it is the worse of the two: matters do not stand so well with mankind that the majority should prefer the better course: the more people do a thing the worse it is likely to be. Let us therefore inquire, not what is most commonly done, but what is best for us to do, and what will establish us in the possession of undying happiness, not what is approved of by the vulgar, the worst possible exponents of truth. By "the vulgar" I mean both those who wear woollen cloaks and those who wear crowns; for I do not regard the colour of the clothes with which they are covered: I do not trust my eyes to tell me what a man is: I have a better and more trustworthy light by which I can distinguish what is true from what is false: let the mind find out what is good for the mind.

plain_english: If a man ever gives his mind some room to breathe and has time to be alone with himself, what truths he will admit to himself! It's like being tortured by his own thoughts. He will say, "I wish I could undo everything I've done so far. When I think about what I've said, I envy people who can't speak. Everything I've wanted seems like something my enemies would pray would happen to me. Good God, what I feared turns out to be so much more bearable than what I craved. I've been enemies with many people, then turned my hatred into friendship — if you can call it friendship when both people are bad. But I still haven't made peace with myself.
original_excerpt: If a man ever allows his mind some breathing space and has leisure for communing with himself, what truths he will confess to himself, after having been put to the torture by his own self! He will say, "Whatever I have hitherto done I wish were undone: when I think over what I have said, I envy dumb people: whatever I have longed for seems to have been what my enemies would pray might befall me: good heaven, how far more endurable what I have feared seems to be than what I have lusted after. I have been at enmity with many men, and have changed my dislike of them into friendship, if friendship can exist between bad men: yet I have not yet become reconciled to myself.

plain_english: I worked as hard as I could to rise above ordinary people. I wanted to stand out for some special talent. But what did I accomplish? I just made myself a target for my enemies. I showed them exactly where to hurt me. Look around you. See those people who praise your speaking skills? The ones who want your money, seek your favor, or brag about your power? They're all your enemies. Or they might as well be. For every person who admires you, there's someone who envies you. So why don't I look for something good that I can actually use and enjoy? Something that's mine, not something to show off? These flashy things that people stare at in wonder — the things crowds gather to see, that leave people speechless with admiration — they shine on the outside. But inside, they make their owners miserable.
original_excerpt: I have striven with all my strength to raise myself above the common herd, and to make myself remarkable for some talent: what have I effected save to make myself a mark for the arrows of my enemies, and show those who hate me where to wound me? Do you see those who praise your eloquence, who covet your wealth, who court your favour, or who vaunt your power? All these either are, or, which comes to the same thing, may be your enemies: the number of those who envy you is as great as that of those who admire you; why do I not rather seek for some good thing which I can use and feel, not one which I can show? these good things which men gaze at in wonder, which they crowd to see, which one points out to another with speechless admiration, are outwardly brilliant, but within are miseries to those who possess them."
